name: Lucas Palma
bio:
Lucas Palma is an Information Security Manager at Nubank, one of the world’s largest digital financial services platforms, where he leads Product Security across Application Security, Mobile Security, AI Security, and Product Security Engineering. He works at the intersection of software engineering, product security, and AI, helping teams adopt AI safely without slowing down product development.

His current work focuses on securing AI adoption at enterprise scale, including AI coding assistants, agentic workflows, MCP integrations, secure coding guidance, AI security tooling, and automated security review inside developer workflows. He has more than 15 years of experience in information security, software engineering, and financial services, with work ranging from building security programs from scratch to reducing banking malware incidents by 90 percent through layered mobile protections.

Lucas is passionate about making security practical for engineers by turning real attack patterns into guardrails, automation, evaluations, and tools that help teams ship faster and safer.

positions.claim: AI skills should be governed as supply chain dependencies rather than as configuration files.
Security effort should protect the entire developer workflow, not just the generated code.
A skill author effectively controls the code generated on other engineers' machines, which is a distinct and dangerous trust transfer.
Deterministic scanning alone is insufficient and LLM review alone is unreliable, so a hybrid of both is required; LLM verdicts vary with temperature.
Local scanning must be re-enforced in CI because you cannot ensure the engineer ran the checks or ran the latest version.
Findings should be delivered in the same pull request that uploads the skill, because co-locating feedback improves usability.
Nubank scanned over 2,000 skills, found more than 1,500 risks, saw about 1,000 remediated immediately, and blocked a few before marketplace distribution.
A prompt instruction to 'ask for confirmation' does not constitute a human in the loop, because the agent can satisfy the confirmation itself.
Treating all shell commands as equally risky produced poor results; risk must be graded per command.
Low-context, weak signals cause more trouble than they are worth in a skill scanner.
Findings without clear remediation guidance are counterproductive.
The same review approach generalizes to plugins, MCP servers, agent rules, and hooks, though with different risk classes.
Third-party skills downloaded from outside should be routed through the internal marketplace so they get scanned before use.
A single canonical marketplace is a fragile chokepoint because teams can spin up other marketplaces, requiring proactive discovery.
